summary: When Pokemon GO launched in 2016, player traffic reached 50 times Niantic's initial target and ten times its worst-case estimate within days. Google Cloud and Niantic scaled the Kubernetes backend with tens of thousands of cores.

overview.background: Niantic ran Pokemon GO on Google Cloud: Cloud Datastore as the main database, Google Container Engine (GKE) with Kubernetes for application logic, and Google's global network. The team planned for 1X traffic with a 5X worst case.
systems: Network load balancer then HTTP/S load balancer
Google's global network and Cloud services
overview.impact: Within 15 minutes of launching in Australia and New Zealand traffic was past Niantic's expectations. Traffic reached 50X the target.
overview.severity: A capacity incident rather than an outage. Google describes stability issues that were worked through in sequence.
overview.gaps: The post gives no error rates or exact downtime.

timeline.t: Launch day, Australia and New Zealand
timeline.e: Pokemon GO launches in the first countries.
Player traffic is well past Niantic's expectations.
Traffic reaches 50X the target, ten times the worst-case estimate.
Google's customer reliability engineers provision extra capacity on Niantic's behalf.
A newer GKE version allows more than a thousand extra nodes, and the Network Load Balancer is replaced by the HTTP/S Load Balancer.
Sign-ups triple the earlier US launch numbers and the launch goes smoothly.

rootCause.trigger: Traffic far above the worst-case estimate after a successful launch.
rootCause.underlying: Capacity and load balancer design planned for 5X could not carry 50X without upgrades and extra provisioning.
contributing: The cluster size limit of the earlier GKE version
The load balancer type was a poor fit for HTTPS traffic
Launch timing in several countries gave little time to react
propagation: Capacity is added and design changed.

evidence.label: Surge size
evidence.body: Pokémon GO's popularity quickly surged player traffic to 50X the initial target, ten times the worst-case estimate.

evidence.label: Early signal
evidence.body: Within 15 minutes of launching in Australia and New Zealand, player traffic surged well past Niantic's expectations.

evidence.label: A simulated autoscaling policy
evidence.note: Shows headroom-based scaling settings. Invented values.

diagnose.step: Compare real traffic with the plan.
diagnose.why: 50X against 5X shows the scale of the miss.

diagnose.step: Check cluster node limits and quotas.
diagnose.why: A newer GKE version raised the node count.

diagnose.step: Check load balancer behaviour for your protocol.

correct.step: Provision extra capacity ahead of growth.
Upgrade to a version with higher limits.
correct.why: More than a thousand extra nodes.

verify.step: Watch error rates and latency as capacity arrives.
verify.why: Stability issues were worked through in sequence.

verify.step: Run the next launch as a test of the new capacity.

prevent.step: Plan for ten times the worst case.

prevent.why: Regional launches gave time to react.

prevent.step: Keep platform engineers close to the launch.

fix.safety: Upgrading a cluster version in the middle of a surge is risky. Rehearse the upgrade and keep a rollback path.

troubleshoot.scenario: Your game is three days from a global launch. A small region launched and traffic is already 10 times the estimate.
troubleshoot.question: What do you do before the next launch?
troubleshoot.answer: Upgrade to a version with higher node limits, switch to a fitting load balancer, provision extra capacity, engage the provider's reliability engineers, and launch the next region as a test.

rootcause.q: What was the worst-case estimate relative to target?
rootcause.why: Teams planned for about 5X as worst case.

remediation.answer: Provision for ten times the worst case with fast scale-up.
Use an HTTP/S balancer for HTTPS traffic.
Smaller regions first, with a gap to learn.

design.prompt: Design a backend that tolerates a launch 50X above plan.
design.answer: Use headroom, horizontal scale, a database that scales, staged launches, load shedding and a vendor on call.
